21644-every-man-for-himself:
Hopkins Moorhouse opens Every Man for Himself in fog on Front Street, Toronto, in a tale copyrighted in Canada in 1920. A lone policeman writes in his patrol book under an arc light. A young athlete strides out of the gray vapour toward the docks.

Chapters turn on a tan satchel that keeps reappearing at key moments. A listening stenographer, a private car named Obaska, and trouble on the Winnipeg Express drive the plot. Kendrick makes a touchdown, McCorquodale explains, and a race begins. Moorhouse, who wrote Deep Furrows of the prairie west, here spins a brisk tale of money and mystery.
22526-cubs-of-the-wolf:
Cubs of the Wolf is a science fiction story preserved from Project Gutenberg. Its characters argue about ridicule aimed at their own profession. Specialists, one complains, are the butt of enough ridicule already now.

Do something foolish, he warns, and the ridicule follows for life. Knees knock whenever anyone inquires about your specialty afterward. Worse, they threaten to read your thesis aloud in public. That academic dread gives the tale a wry, knowing start. Wolf cubs, by the title, suggest young predators or young trainees. Readers get a period story where status anxiety meets strange science. Its humor comes from experts fearing embarrassment more than danger.
ardath-the-story-of-a-dead-self:
Marie Corelli's Ardath: The Story of a Dead Self opens in a monastery deep in the Caucasus. A storm gathers over the Pass of Dariel as night approaches, and Mount Kazbek rises coldly white. Part one bears the title Saint and Sceptic. The sceptic is Theos Alwyn, a young poet whose fame has not saved his faith.

Alwyn seeks the monk Heliobas, whose learning joins holiness to strange science. Under his guidance the poet's spirit travels to Al-Kyris, a lost city of the ancient world. There he meets the self he was in a former life, and the woman he loved and wronged. Corelli builds her romance on reincarnation and the soul's long education. Ardath was her most ambitious occult novel, preached with a prophet's certainty. Its Caucasus storm and phantom city frame a gospel of spiritual evolution.
beowulf:
Francis Barton Gummere translated Beowulf, the Old English epic of the Geatish hero, into alliterative English verse that keeps the original's hammering rhythm. The prelude praises Scyld Scefing, founder of the Danish house, who waxed under heaven until far peoples gave him gifts. His descendant Hrothgar builds Heorot, the great hall Grendel attacks.

Beowulf crosses the whale-path to Denmark, wrestles Grendel in the gabled hall, dives to fight Grendel's mother, and in old age faces a dragon at home. Gummere's diction, athelings, mead-benches, and hall-thanes, gives modern readers the poem's strangeness without a crib. His version served generations of students as the standard verse translation of England's oldest epic.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-aloys-lutolf:
Aloys Lutolf, historian, was born at Gettnau near Willisau in 1824 and died at Lucerne in 1879. He studied at Schwyz's Jesuit College and Lucerne's Lyceum, keen on history. Politics barred serious study, so Lütolf and fellow students volunteered. He served as Lucerne private secretary and joined the Sonderbund's Ticino expedition. From 1847 to 1849 he read theology and history at Freiburg and Munich, ordained at Solothurn.

After mission service, he taught at St. Gall's cantonal school from 1852 to 1856. When the school closed, he became Lucerne parish priest. He became church history professor in 1858, Lucerne's St. Leodegar canon, and Solothurn seminary viceregent in 1864. In 1859 he began publishing St. Gall investigations. Chief are Legends, Customs and Tales from the Five Places (1865) and Heralds of the Faith in Switzerland before St. Gall (1870), a contribution to ancient Swiss history. His Life and Confessions of Schiffmann (1861) memorializes his master and covers Bishop Sailer and his Swiss school.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-arculf:
Arculf, a Frankish bishop of the later seventh century, is known through Bede's account of a pilgrimage that became a book. Some, such as Alexis de Gourgues, call him bishop of Périgueux, but most believe he belonged to some monastery. Bede relates that Arculf, returning from the Holy Land about 670 or 690, was cast by tempest on the Scottish shore and warmly received by Adamnan, abbot of Iona.

To Adamnan he gave a detailed narrative of his Holy Land travels, with plans and designs of the sanctuaries precise enough that Adamnan could produce a descriptive work. With help from other sources, Adamnan produced that work in three books on Jerusalem, Bethlehem, the chief towns of Palestine, and Constantinople. Adamnan gave a copy to Aldfrith, king of Northumbria, in 698. The work aims to report faithfully what Arculf actually saw, joined to an antiquary's zeal.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ceolwulf:
Ceolwulf, also spelled Ceolwulph or Ceolulph, was king of Northumbria and monk of Lindisfarne, dying at Lindisfarne in 764; his birth date and place are unknown. The Anglo-Saxon Chronicle traces his ancestry back through Cutha, Cuthwin, Leoldwald, Egwald, Aldhelm, and Ocga to Ida and Eoppa. Most authorities say Osric adopted him as heir in 729, though Harpsfeld says he succeeded Osred.

Learned and pious, he lacked the vigor and authority a ruler needs. Bede witnesses to his learning and piety in the opening chapter of his Ecclesiastical History, dedicated to the most glorious King Ceolwulph and sent for his approval. His subjects seized him in his second regnal year and confined him in a monastery, but he escaped and regained the throne. He made his cousin Egbert Bishop of York, and his feast day is 15 January.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-cynewulf:
A literary entry examines Cynewulf, the Anglo-Saxon poet whose authorship is certain yet whose identity is not. He signed four poems by spelling his name in runic letters that read as sense within the verse. Who he was remains uncertain. Good reason links him with Cynewulf, Bishop of Lindisfarne.

A rival claim favours Cynulf, an ecclesiastic who signed the decrees of Clovesho in 803. But the chief argument against the bishop has been shown baseless. It claimed a debt to Alcuin's work of about 802. From his own runic passages we learn he knew revelry in a hall, was converted, and gave himself to sacred song, dreading past sins in old age. His certain poems are Christ, Elene, Juliana, and the Fates of the Apostles.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ernulf: This 1913 reference piece on Ernulf — the Bishop of Rochester. Thomas Poole honors his famous Textus. His pen ordered the cathedral's charters. The Normans knew their learned prelate. The architect of the Norman choir. His 1115 see is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-golden-calf: This 1913 reference article on the Golden Calf — the desert idol. James F. Driscoll unfolds its scriptural shame. Aaron cast the molten god. Moses ground the guilty gold. The apostasy of the Sinai camp. Its Exodus tale is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-ingulf: This 1913 reference article on Ingulf — the Abbot of Croyland. Oswald Hunter-Blair honors his famous chronicle. His pen chronicled the Norman age. The scholars mine his vivid pages. A monk among the historians. His 1109 death is famed.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-st-bertulf: St. Bertulf, the monk of the 600s, kept the Frankish rule. This brief entry notes his life and his sanctity. A quiet name from the Merovingian cloisters: his lonely cell crowned the abbey in the 600s' Gaul in the north.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-theodulf: Theodulf was the bishop of Orléans. This long entry examines his 700s, his capitularies, and his fall. The Goth of the Carolingian court: his famed capitularies crowned Orléans in the 800s of the Charlemagne in the truly very old court.
doe-osti-3009665-review-of-presentation-: Carter Wolf's presentation got reviewed, and this DOE text covers the assessment. The pages detail the findings. The researchers get their record. The presenter was Carter Wolf. The record was researcher. The assessment was review. The text was DOE's. The review was DOE's.
doe-osti-3374079-analysis-of-temperature: Neutron detectors got temperature-analyzed, and this DOE text covers self-powered gamma. The pages detail the effects findings. The nuclear folks get their data. The field was gamma. The data were nuclear. The self-powered were detectors. The temperature were analysis.
fanny-herself:
Edna Ferber wrote Fanny Herself as a novel about Fanny Brandeis, a Jewish girl growing up in a Wisconsin town where her widowed mother runs a dry-goods bazaar. Fanny is bright, funny, and unsentimental, and she refuses the ladylike future others plan for her. After her mother dies, she leaves home and builds a career as a buyer for a Chicago mail-order house.

Ferber fills the middle chapters with the workings of that mail-order business, its bundle chutes, stock clerks, and orders bound for Alaska and Georgia. Fanny succeeds through nerve and taste, then faces a harder choice between money, ambition, and the people she loves. Readers get a sharp portrait of a self-made businesswoman in early twentieth-century America.
little-eyolf:
Henrik Ibsen wrote this play in Christiania during 1894. Copenhagen published it on December 11 that year. William Archer translated it and supplied this introduction. Archer notes Ibsen's correspondence offers few clues to its origins.

One character, the Rat-Wife, has a definite suggested model. An old woman killed rats at Ibsen's childhood school. She carried a little dog in a bag, Ibsen told Prozor. Children were said to have drowned following her, like Hamelin's piper. Archer admits very little anecdotic history attaches to the play. Prozor's French word infatuation puzzles him in Allmers's case.
richard-dare-s-venture-or-striking-out-f:
Edward Stratemeyer tells boys how Richard Dare struck out for himself, in a preface to the revised edition dated at Newark on March 1, 1899. The book is complete in itself, he says, yet opens his Bound to Succeed series. Readers and critics across the country had taken it warmly, to his surprise and thanks.

Richard is a country youth who finds nothing to do in his sleepy village and goes to New York to seek his fortune. He has almost no cash, but backbone and his mother's Christian teaching in plenty. City life proves no bed of roses, and snares meet him once he gains a footing. The New York street scenes, Stratemeyer adds, are taken from life.
the-complete-poems-of-sir-thomas-moore-c:
Sir Thomas Moore's complete poems, collected by himself with explanatory notes, open with a biographical sketch by William M. Rossetti. The sketch begins with the poet's birth in Dublin on the 28th of May, 1780, as the date is printed there.

His father was a grocer and spirit-retailer, called a spirit-grocer in Ireland. Thomas was schooled by Mr. Samuel Whyte, once Sheridan's first teacher, a man of more than average literary culture. Whyte encouraged acting among the boys, and Moore, bright and lively by nature, became a favorite and a leader in the school plays. His gift for verse showed early. In 1790 he wrote an epilogue for a piece acted at Lady Borrows's house in Dublin, and at fourteen he published a sonnet to Whyte in a Dublin magazine. Rossetti frames the poems with that rise from a tradesman's son to a national poet.
the-golden-calf: M. E. Braddon wrote The Golden Calf. It is a novel. The title page names Braddon as author of Lady Audley's Secret and Aurora Floyd. It names Vixen and Ishmael as well. Only front matter is present here. It gives the title page and a contents list. The heads open with The Articled Pupil. One head is blunt: I Am Going to Marry for Money. Later heads name Wendover Abbey, a birthday feast, and a solemn league. They name Kingthorpe society and The True Knight.
the-great-panjandrum-himself: The Great Panjandrum Himself is one of R. Caldecott's Picture Books. Frederick Warne and Company published the series. Only the opening pages are present here: the front cover and the first picture pages. The book is a nonsense rhyme told in pictures. A lady goes into the garden to cut a cabbage-leaf, to make an apple-pie. The words come a line or two at a time, under the pictures. No more of the rhyme is present.
the-half-back-a-story-of-school-football: Ralph Henry Barbour wrote The Half-Back, a story of school, football, and golf, with pictures by B. West Clinedinst. The dedication speaks to every American boy who loves honest, manly sport. Chapter titles in the contents include The Boy in the Straw Hat, Station Road and River Path, Outfield West, The Head Coach, The Practice Game, and The Golf Tournament. Nothing past the front matter is present here.
the-history-of-thomas-ellwood-written-by:
The History of Thomas Ellwood was written by Ellwood himself. George Routledge and Sons printed the edition in 1885. Henry Morley wrote an introduction for it. Morley presents the life of the simple Quaker with praise. The book makes Ellwood known with frankness, he says. It also brings a bygone time close to the reader. It even helps the reader come near to Milton in daily life.

Ellwood was born in 1639, in the reign of Charles the First. His story runs to 1683, when he was forty-four. He outlived the days of trouble recorded in the book. He died on the first of March 1713, aged seventy-four. His house stood at Hunger Hill.
the-son-of-the-wolf:
Jack London's 1900 collection gathers nine tales of the far north. Among them are The White Silence, The Men of Forty Mile, In a Far Country, and The Wisdom of the Trail. An Odyssey of the North completes the set. The title story gives the volume its name, and the harsh Yukon world runs through the whole set.

The White Silence opens with Mason tending a failing sled dog, Carmen, while Malemute Kid thaws frozen bread by the fire. Ruth, Mason's Indian wife, listens in silence. Two hundred miles of trail lie ahead, with six days of food for the people and none for the dogs, so hunger shapes every choice the party faces.
toward-the-gulf: Edgar Lee Masters gathered poems under his title in a contents list running from the title poem through lake boats, cities of the plain, Johnny Appleseed, and a loom. Dialogue at Perko's, Sir Galahad, St. Deseret, and Victor Rafolski on art appear among the titles. Later poems treat dahlias, the Grand River marshes, Delilah, France, Christmas at Indian Point, and a clinical lecture by Dr. Scudder. A contents list alone is held in this record, so Masters's poems themselves are not shown.
when-a-man-comes-to-himself:
Woodrow Wilson wrote the essay When a Man Comes to Himself in 1901. Wilson, who later served as President of the United States, treats a quiet inner change. A man comes to himself, he says, not only after wild or foolish years. The change can follow private trials that no one else has seen.

Such a man stops centering all his plans on himself. He sees the world as it is and finds his true place in it. Old illusions drop away, both the rosy ones and the dark ones. He learns his own pace and the roads he must run. Wilson calls the loss of illusion a gain, since the new light guides rather than cheats.
